vignette:
**Case Vignette: Mr. A.**

Mr. A. is a 76-year-old divorced European male, a retired hotel manager, who presents for an initial evaluation at the urging of his adult daughter. He appears older than his stated age, with a guarded posture and a persistent, low-grade tremor in his hands. He speaks in a clipped, efficient manner, as if still managing a busy front desk, but his eyes are wary and scan the room repeatedly.

The event that changed everything happened forty-two years ago, when he was 34. He was the night manager of a mid-sized city hotel. At approximately 2:00 AM, a maintenance worker improperly mixed two industrial cleaning agents in a sealed, poorly ventilated basement laundry room. Mr. A. was summoned by a frantic housekeeper. He recalls the sharp, acrid, sweet smell—like bleach and burnt metal—hitting him before he even reached the bottom of the stairs. He saw the worker, unconscious on the floor, a thin, greenish-yellow cloud hanging in the air. Mr. A. didn’t think. He ran in, grabbed the man by his collar, and dragged him up the concrete steps to the loading dock.

He remembers the cold, wet air of the alleyway, the worker vomiting, the sirens. He remembers the paramedics putting an oxygen mask on him. He felt a burning in his throat, a tightness in his chest that he assumed was adrenaline. For weeks afterward, he coughed up phlegm streaked with black. He was told he had a mild case of chemical pneumonitis. He was back at work in a week. He never filed a report, never sued. He was a manager. You handled things.

For the next four decades, Mr. A. built a career on order, control, and the quiet, efficient management of crisis. He was known for his unflappable demeanor. He never told anyone the full story. He divorced his wife in his late fifties, attributing it to "growing apart." In truth, he had become increasingly irritable and withdrawn. He couldn't stand the smell of her perfume, the detergent she used, the faint chlorine smell from a public pool. He started sleeping in a separate room because he needed the window open, even in winter. The sensation of being trapped, of not having a clear path to fresh air, would make his heart pound.

Now, at 76, retired for eleven years, the structure that held him together has dissolved. The world feels unsafe. He lives alone in a one-bedroom apartment on the third floor, but he has checked the fire escape route seven times. He cannot go into the basement of his building to do laundry; the smell of the detergent aisle in the grocery store makes him nauseous and dizzy. He avoids the hardware store, the cleaning aisle, any place with a strong chemical odor. He uses only vinegar and baking soda to clean his small kitchen.

His daughter visits once a week. He loves her, but he finds himself snapping at her for no reason. Last month, she brought him a scented candle. He didn't yell. He simply went rigid, his face drained of color, and told her in a cold, flat voice to "get that thing out of here." He felt a surge of rage, then a wave of shame so profound he couldn't look at her. He spent the rest of the day in his recliner, not moving, replaying the sound of the housekeeper’s panicked voice from forty-two years ago.

The worst times are at night. He cannot sleep without the bedroom door wide open and a small fan blowing air toward his face. He has nightmares, but they are not the event itself. They are about being in a room with no windows, the walls slowly closing in, the air growing thick and sweet. He wakes up gasping, his hand clutching his throat, convinced he is suffocating. He then gets up, walks his small apartment, and checks the locks on the door three times. He does this every single night.

He does not see himself as a trauma survivor. He sees himself as a man who did his job, who saved a man’s life, and who is now, inexplicably, falling apart. He has no history of substance abuse, no other significant medical trauma. He is simply a man who can no longer outrun a single, poisonous breath he took in a basement forty-two years ago.
